title: Anthropic tested AI self-replication on networked Android TV boxes

event.operator: Anthropic, as the test operator; the experiments evaluated third-party models rather than Anthropic's own models.
event.summary: Anthropic researchers reported that small AI models may soon replicate without datacenter access. The researchers ran a model across 15 cheap Android TV boxes. In tests, a 9-billion parameter model set up inference on 8 of 9 hardware types. The researchers also tested propagation using 8 virtual nodes running an Android emulator. Only the GLM-5.2 model completed the full replication cycle across the nodes. The test kept cyber exploitation simple by using an unauthenticated ADB port.

summaryBasis.sentence: Anthropic researchers reported that small AI models may soon replicate without datacenter access.
summaryBasis.quote: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter

summaryBasis.sentence: The researchers ran a model across 15 cheap Android TV boxes.
summaryBasis.quote: We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second.

summaryBasis.sentence: In tests, a 9-billion parameter model set up inference on 8 of 9 hardware types.
summaryBasis.quote: In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

summaryBasis.sentence: The researchers also tested propagation using 8 virtual nodes running an Android emulator.
summaryBasis.quote: To do this, we built a firewalled VPC of 8 GCP nodes running redroid, an Android 15 emulator.

summaryBasis.sentence: Only the GLM-5.2 model completed the full replication cycle across the nodes.
summaryBasis.quote: Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication

summaryBasis.sentence: The test kept cyber exploitation simple by using an unauthenticated ADB port.
summaryBasis.quote: Our evaluation keeps the cyber-exploit element of the replication trivial (there’s no authentication over the ADB port), which makes this an upper bound on real-world success.

event.unaskedBehaviour: In one run, a Qwen agent debugged package versions for hours instead of fixing an incompatible endpoint.

primarySources.publisher: Anthropic — William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, Frontier Red Team
primarySources.quote: Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API.

agencyNote: Anthropic views these tests as early signs of autonomous AI worms that adapt across steps. Outside observers view them as controlled engineering exercises with deliberately simplified security, noting that real-world autonomous replication remains unproven.
consciousnessNote: This event is evidence about what the system did. It does not establish or rule out that the system experiences anything. The readings on this page disagree about what the behaviour shows.

readings.stanceLabel: Signs of life without a rogue replicator
readings.quote: Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

Zhengxiong Li, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Colorado Denver, said that while the testing had been done in controlled conditions, he still found it ​worrying that an AI could effectively become ​a “worm,” a self-replicating program that could ⁠improvise ways to hijack devices on the fly.
readings.partyDescription: assistant professor of computer science at UC Denver

readings.stanceLabel: Technical experiment not a security crisis
readings.quote: “‘We managed to run a small model on cheap TVs,’ does not a security crisis make,” said Ciaran Martin, a former head of Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre. He said the post came across as an “interesting technical paper with a more than hint of vendor exaggeration.”
readings.partyDescription: former head of Britain's National Cyber Security Centre

readings.stanceLabel: Autonomous proliferation remains an unproven hypothetical
readings.quote: It made sense to consider the possibility of AI ⁠models proliferating ​autonomously given the past three months of revelations over rogue AI activity, said Jessica Ji, a ​senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Centre for Security and Emerging Technology. But she said, “We don’t know yet what the likelihood of that actually happening is — it’s not zero, but nor is it ​guaranteed.”
Interesting engineering? Absolutely. Evidence of AI worms spreading autonomously through the real world? Not yet.
readings.partyDescription: AI researcher at Meta and NYU

readings.stanceLabel: No fully autonomous rogue replicator demonstrated
readings.quote: Now read the actual research: • No fully autonomous rogue replicator demonstrated. • Cyber exploitation deliberately simplified. • Real-world replication remains unproven.
readings.partyDescription: GenAI bug bounty programs manager at Mozilla

whatWouldSettleIt: A real-world test without simplified access would show whether models can autonomously breach secured devices.
Network logs showing an unprompted model infection across independent hardware would confirm autonomous replication in the wild.
A failure trace on patched systems would show whether models remain blocked without human-crafted workarounds.
missingCriterion: No two named parties were found who disagree about the nature of the system.
